# Dots & Boxes: Brain Duel

> A free Android version of the classic dots and boxes pen-and-paper game, by Sujan Shrestha (Kathmandu, Nepal). No ads, no in-app purchases, no tracking. Play the computer through eight worlds with their own twists and bosses, solve a daily puzzle, pass the phone around with 2 to 6 players, or play online in private, public and ranked rooms.

- Get it on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sujanshrestha.dotsandboxes
- Platform: Android only (no iPhone version yet)
- Price: free; no ads; no in-app purchases
- Players: 1 to 6
- Offline: games against the computer, the daily puzzle, Chain School and Pass & Play work without internet
- Online: random opponents, private rooms with a 6-letter code, public rooms, friends and invites, ranked ratings and a leaderboard; the server checks every move
- Computer levels: Beginner, Casual, Skilled, Expert, Master (Master calculates the endgame exactly)
- Worlds: after 8 training levels come eight worlds of 8 levels each (Clover Meadow, Frostpeak Pass, Sunscorch Dunes, Coral Deep, Ember Peaks, Cloud Isles, Lantern City, Starfall Orbit), each with its own twist (such as hedge mazes, frozen lines or gold boxes worth 2), new board shapes and a boss; then the worlds return as harder laps, so levels never run out
- Daily puzzle: a new endgame each day, the same for everyone, worth up to 3 stars
- Chain School: twelve puzzles that teach chains, sacrifices and the double-cross
- Board styles: Paper, Chalkboard and Neon, unlocked with trophies; light and dark themes
- Privacy: no email, phone number or location needed; online play uses an anonymous account that can be deleted from Settings

## How to play dots and boxes

1. Start with a grid of dots. Players take turns drawing one line between two neighbouring dots.
2. Closing the fourth side of a box claims it, and that player draws another line.
3. When every line is drawn, the player with the most boxes wins.

## How to win

- Avoid drawing the third side of a box early on: the opponent takes it and moves again.
- When the safe moves run out, the board splits into chains of boxes; whoever must open the first long chain usually loses.
- Double-cross: when taking a long chain, leave the last two boxes; the opponent takes them and must open the next chain.
- Sacrificing a short chain can force the opponent to open the long ones.
